GSoC 2026 · ML4Sci · Weekly Update

Point-Cloud Super-Resolution
for Calorimeter Jet Images

Building a set-to-set model that treats a jet as a list of hits rather than a dense image — and what measuring it honestly revealed.

Rajveer Rathod · Week of 15–22 September 2026
Headline: the pipeline is built, tested and measured end to end. It does not yet beat the grid baseline — and the figures produced this week locate exactly which change broke it.
Slide 2

Where this fits

Two parallel pipelines, one repository.

Grid pipeline — shipped, working

A CNN GAN on dense (3,128,128) images. Tagging efficiency 89.7%, recovery +44.8%. Untouched by this work and its tests stay green.

Point-cloud pipeline — this update

A from-scratch set-to-set transformer: LR hit list → HR hit list, never touching a dense image internally. A second, parallel research effort — not an incremental change.

Why attempt a point cloud at all

Calorimeter data is 98.5% empty pixels (measured, not assumed). On that data a plain pixel-wise L1 loss is minimised by outputting a dim blob, because empty pixels dominate the average. The grid pipeline fixed this with an engineered workaround (energy-weighted L1, alpha=5.0).

A loss defined over a list of actual hits has no empty-pixel dilution to exploit, so the degenerate optimum disappears by construction rather than by tuning. That was the hypothesis worth testing.

Hit representation

Every hit is 4 numbers: (channel, x, y, energy). Lists are padded to a fixed budget with a boolean mask, so a batch is one tensor. Budgets come from a data audit — HR carries 744 hits/jet on average, so hr_n_max=1300 is the 99th percentile, not a guess.

Fixed output budget + learned existence score, the DETR pattern: the model emits 1300 candidate slots and learns which are real, rather than generating a variable-length list. Variable-length generation is substantially harder to train; the cost of this choice is the matching problem on slide 8.
Architecture4
Slide 5

The generator

SetGenerator — encoder, queries, cross-attention decoder.

1 · Encoder

PermInvariantEncoder, Deep-Sets style: a per-point MLP followed by a masked mean+max pool. Permutation-invariant by construction — reordering the input hit list cannot change the output.

2 · Queries

1300 output slots, each seeded from a real LR hit position (round-robin tiled, with a learned per-repeat perturbation so repeats of the same seed can specialise).

3 · Decoder

3-layer transformer decoder, 4 heads, d_model=128. Queries cross-attend to the full per-hit LR sequence plus one global summary token.

Per-slot output head

x, y = sigmoid(·) × (grid−1) Always a valid HR coordinate, by construction.
energy = softplus(·) Non-negative — calorimeter deposits cannot be negative.
existence = raw logit Thresholded only at final rasterisation, never inside the loss.
channel = argmax(3-way softmax) Discrete; gradient flows via the cross-entropy term instead.
Discriminator (SetDiscriminator) judges “is this a plausible HR set given this LR set” from the pooled encoding only — a deliberately global judgement, since a point cloud has no patches to run a PatchGAN over.
Architecture · generator5
Slide 6

Loss functions

Five terms. The first is the reconstruction workhorse.

Masked Chamfer — the main reconstruction term

L_chamfer = meanp mint D(p,t)  +  Σt wt · minp D(p,t) / Σt wt Both directions: every prediction must be near some target, and every target must be covered by some prediction. Padded targets are excluded from the search entirely.
D(p,t) = ||xyp − xyt||²  +  λE · |Ep − Et|     wt = 1 + α·Et Position distance PLUS an explicit energy-value gap, and target-side weighting by energy (same alpha=5.0 as the grid pipeline's weighted L1). Both were added after a measured failure — see slide 7.

Existence — BCE

Is this slot a real hit? Teaches cardinality instead of imposing it. Weight 1.0.

Channel — cross-entropy

Which of 3 calorimeter channels, masked to real hits. Weight 0.1.

Energy conservation

|ΣE_pred / ΣE_true − 1| — identical to the grid pipeline's physics loss. Weight 1.0.

Adversarial — LSGAN

Weight 0.1, with a 3-epoch warm-up then a 5-epoch ramp, so reconstruction settles first.

Sinkhorn (entropic optimal transport) is implemented and wired as an alternative to Chamfer — it penalises many-to-one collapses that Chamfer permits — but is off by default at ~3× the compute. Its benefit has not been isolated; that remains an open experiment.
Loss functions6
Slide 7

Fix 1: the loss had no opinion about energy

Symptom, found by measurement

A position-only Chamfer loss produced SR jets whose top-5 energies were flat (10.9, 9.2, 7.4, 6.2, 6.1) against HR's peaked profile (27.6, 16.6, 6.2, 6.0, 4.0) — while matching total energy closely.

Root cause

Nearest-neighbour matching on (x,y) gives zero gradient pressure on whether the matched energy value is right. So “spread the same total energy across more, dimmer hits” was a valid low-loss solution — the Chamfer analogue of the grid pipeline's “predict small everywhere”.

Fix

Add the |E_p − E_t| term and energy-weight the target side (slide 6). The same bug was found and fixed independently in Sinkhorn, whose transport masses are normalised per sample and therefore see only each hit's relative share, never its absolute value.

Tagging efficiency moved 69.7% → 70.9%. The fix was correct and verified — and the metric that matters barely moved. This pattern repeats, and is the story of this update.
Fix 1 · energy-value term7
Slide 8

Fixes 2–4: conditioning and correspondence

Fix 2 (Stage A) — attention bottleneck

The model pooled the entire ~600-hit LR set into one 128-number vector, then every output slot attended to that single token. Softmax over a length-1 memory has weight exactly 1.0, always — so no slot could attend differently from any other.

Fix: cross-attend to the full per-hit LR sequence + a summary token, with padding masked.

Fix 3 (Stage B) — blank queries

All 1300 output slots started from the same fixed vector in every sample, carrying zero information about that jet.

Fix: seed each query from an actual LR hit position, with a learned per-repeat perturbation so slots seeded from one hit can specialise to different nearby HR hits.

Fix 4 (Stage C) — this week

Existence and channel losses compared predicted slot i to target row i. But a point cloud is unordered — row order is an arbitrary storage detail. The same jet with shuffled rows gave a different loss.

Fix: Hungarian matching before those two losses.

Why Stage C's bug stayed hidden: Chamfer does its own nearest-neighbour matching, so it was never affected. One loss term was doing real matching while another was supervising against noise — and the healthy-looking Chamfer curve masked it.
Fixes 2–48
Slide 9

Stage C in detail — Hungarian matching

The algorithm

  • Per sample, build a cost matrix between all 1300 predicted slots and all real target hits, using squared (x,y) distance.
  • Solve with scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment — an optimal one-to-one assignment, not a greedy nearest-neighbour pass.
  • Targets are canonically ordered before solving, so the solver's tie-breaking cannot depend on storage order either.
  • Unmatched predictions → supervised toward non-existence. Unmatched targets contribute nothing here but are still covered by Chamfer's independent matching.
  • Detached and solved on CPU, up to 4 samples in parallel. Gradients still come from Chamfer — matching only assigns targets.

Cost

2.99 s/batch vs ~2.0 s/batch without — about 50% slower per step, measured rather than estimated.

How it is tested

The regression test mirrors how Fix 1 was pinned — it must fail against the old behaviour and pass against the new:

  • Shuffle the target rows while keeping the underlying set identical. Hungarian matching still recovers the correct correspondence; naive index-order matching does not.
  • Existence and channel loss values are invariant to target row order — false before the fix by construction, true after.
  • No target is ever double-matched.
  • Edge cases: zero real targets, more targets than slots, coincident positions across channels.
  • Parallel and serial solves are bit-identical.
10 new tests. Suite: 108 passed, 1 skipped, with the grid pipeline's own tests green throughout.
Stage C9
Slide 10

How success is measured

Two numbers, and the gap between them is the whole story.

Chamfer distance — the proxy

What the model trains on. Lower is better. Easy to improve, and not what anyone cares about.

Tagging efficiency — the real metric

A jet tagger classifies signal vs background from a calorimeter image. We train one on real HR images, freeze it, then score it on three inputs:

  • HR — the ceiling
  • LR upscaled — the floor, i.e. doing nothing
  • SR — our output
The point-cloud pipeline reuses the grid pipeline's exact frozen tagger code. A parallel tagger would make the two approaches incomparable — a hard constraint, not a convenience.
tagging efficiency = AUCSR / AUCHR How much of the tagger's skill survives when it sees our output instead of the truth.
recovery = (AUCSR − AUCLR) / (AUCHR − AUCLR) Of the distance between "no model" and "perfect", how much did we actually close.
RecoveryMeaning
+100%SR is as good as ground truth
0%SR adds nothing over doing nothing
negativeSR is worse than doing nothing
Recovery is the honest number. Tagging efficiency looks respectable at 70% even while the model is actively destroying information. Reporting efficiency alone would have hidden this for weeks.

A diagnostic that was measuring the wrong thing

The broken check

Conditioning was previously assessed by rasterising SR and HR to images and comparing them with cosine similarity. It reported near-total conditioning failure.

On 98.5%-empty data, two point sets differing by only a 2-pixel shift per hit — structurally near-identical, Chamfer distance ~0 — score exactly 0.0 cosine similarity, because sparse pixel overlap needs exact coincidence to register anything.

It was guaranteed to read near-zero regardless of model quality. Conclusions drawn from it were discarded.

The replacement

Measure conditioning in the metric the model actually trains under. For a batch of 16 jets, compute Chamfer from each SR output to every HR target, and ask: is the closest one its own? Chance is 1/16.

CheckpointOwn HRMargin
Stage A (3 ep)14/1639–42%
Stage A+B (3 ep)14/1639–53%
Stage C (5 ep) 16/1668%
Verified across three disjoint batches, not one. Conditioning is excellent — the opposite of what the old diagnostic said. The architecture fixes are not broken.

The finding: peaks died at Stage A

Brightest predicted hit, same jet, same seed, across every checkpoint.

HR truth27.56 0.28206.7—
Fix 1 worked — and Stage A undid it. Peaks were present (43.25, overshooting HR's 27.56) and collapse to ~0.4 from Stage A onward. Loss configuration is identical across these runs (lambda_energy_value: 1.0, chamfer_energy_weighted: true, alpha: 5.0). The change is architectural.

Mean and total energy stay correct throughout. Only the distribution collapses — and distribution is exactly what a jet tagger reads.

Key finding14
Slide 15

Peak collapse, visually

Confound, stated plainly: Fix 1 ran 10 epochs; Stage A/B ran 3. Peaks might need more epochs. Two things argue otherwise — Stage C at 5 epochs reaches a better Chamfer (19.90) than Fix 1 at 10 (21.64) while still flat, and the peak does not grow at all from Stage C epoch 3 to 5 (0.44 → 0.46). A 10-epoch Stage A run would settle it and has not been done.
Key finding · evidence15
Slide 16

What the tagger actually sees

This is the mechanism behind the flat AUC, stated concretely rather than hypothesised: a jet tagger classifies on shower shape and energy concentration. A blob with the right total energy and no concentration gives it nothing to work with. Chamfer does not punish this, because the energy-value term is one penalty averaged over ~750 hit pairs and the vast majority of real HR hits genuinely are dim — getting 750 dim hits approximately right while missing 5 bright ones is a good average and a catastrophic jet.
Mechanism16
Slide 17

Next steps

Reordered by this week's finding — cheapest and most diagnostic first.

1 · Why does Stage A's attention flatten the output?

Now the clearest defect, with a precise location: peaks existed before Stage A and not after, with an unchanged loss. Leading hypothesis — attending over ~600 LR hits lets each output slot average over many inputs, and an averaged prediction is a flat one, where the old single-token memory forced slots to differentiate through the decoder. Cheap checks: per-slot attention entropy, and a 10-epoch Stage A run to close the confound.

2 · Strengthen the energy-value signal (parallel, cheap)

Raise lambda_energy_value above 1.0; weight it by target energy as the position term already is; or add an explicit top-K peak term so bright hits cannot be traded against the dim majority. Loss-weighting only — no architecture change.

3 · Check the rasterisation boundary

Score the tagger on ground-truth HR hits round-tripped through hits_to_dense. If that alone drops AUC, the representation — not the generator — is the bottleneck. ~20 minutes.

4 · Revisit the encoder

Deep-Sets pooling and Chamfer both under-represent local structure, which is what a CNN tagger reads. A hierarchical encoder was scoped out early; the evidence now justifies revisiting.

Next steps17
Slide 18

Summary & open questions

What went well

  • A complete parallel pipeline — data, model, five losses, training, evaluation, diagnostics, figures — built and tested to 108 passing tests, with the shipped grid pipeline untouched.
  • Stage C fixed a real correctness bug: two loss terms were supervising against an arbitrary storage order.
  • A misleading diagnostic was caught and replaced, reversing an earlier conclusion about conditioning.
  • The figures located the regression to a specific architectural change — something four weeks of scalar metrics had not surfaced.

What did not

  • Recovery is −0.8%. The approach does not yet beat doing nothing, and the grid baseline remains far ahead at +44.8%.
  • Three correct fixes bought ~5 points of efficiency. That rate is itself a signal.
Questions for mentors: (1) Is the Stage A attention-averaging hypothesis worth a 10-epoch confirmation run, given ~9 h compute? (2) Should effort continue here, or fold the energy-value lesson back into the grid pipeline? (3) Is a hierarchical (PointNet++ style) encoder in scope for the remaining timeline?
